verdict.justification: A is the stronger operational tracker because its visible capacity calculations, individual allocations, classifications, and dashboard are formula-linked, whereas B presents those calculations as hard-coded values. A also explicitly removes the 15% administrative reserve from available project capacity, a more direct interpretation of the instruction to exclude reserved overhead when determining individual utilization. B instead divides project hours by gross capacity, producing materially different findings—“4 over-utilized, 1 under-utilized” rather than A’s “18 of 23 overutilized, 0 underutilized”—despite displaying an unused 85% available-capacity measure. The department-utilization definition is not fully prescribed, and B’s inclusion of administrative work is defensible; A usefully acknowledges the tension between department and individual thresholds under its chosen method. Both correctly reconcile the project budgets, retain the 23-person registry, and handle Ellen Zhu’s unregistered hours transparently. A’s reusable calculations and clearer application of the overhead reserve outweigh its somewhat longer companion response.

decisive_issues.issue: Formula-linked capacity and utilization calculations make the workbook maintainable as a tracker.
The primary individual classification uses gross capacity rather than capacity remaining after the stated overhead reserve.
